GEO - 2/21 • Structural Geology & Geometric Orientations

Q22: Structural Geology: Attitude of Linear Features & Plunge Mechanics

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Haakon Fossen (Structural Geology, Ch. 2, pp. 24-28); Davis & Reynolds (Structural Geology of Rocks & Regions, Ch. 1)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

22.1 Geometric Description of Linear vs. Planar Geological Features

In structural geology (Haakon Fossen, Structural Geology, Ch. 2, pp. 24–28; Davis & Reynolds, Structural Geology of Rocks and Regions, Ch. 1), the spatial orientation (attitude) of linear and planar elements is strictly distinguished:

Attitude Parameter Geometric Definition Applies To
Plunge The vertical angle between the horizontal plane and a line (or line of maximum elongation), measured downward in a vertical plane Linear features (fold hinge lines, slickenside lineations, mineral stretching lineations)
Trend The compass direction / azimuth of the vertical plane containing a plunging line Linear features
Dip Angle The acute vertical angle between the horizontal plane and an inclined planar surface Planar features (bedding, joints, faults, foliation)
Strike The compass bearing of a horizontal line contained within an inclined geological plane Planar features
Rake (Pitch) The angle between a line and the strike of the plane containing it, measured within the plane Linear features lying on a plane

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q22. The vertical angle between the horizontal plane and the axis or line of maximum elongation of a feature is called ____.
(A) dip angle
(B) strike
(C) right-lateral strike slip
(D) plunge
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (D)

Correct Answer: (D) plunge — The vertical angle between the horizontal plane and a linear feature or axis of maximum elongation is formally defined as the plunge.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) dip angle — INCORRECT: Dip is the vertical angle of inclination of a planar surface (bedding or fault plane), not a linear feature.
  • (B) strike — INCORRECT: Strike is a horizontal compass direction on an inclined plane.
  • (C) right-lateral strike slip — INCORRECT: A kinematic fault displacement sense (dextral strike-slip), not an orientation angle.
  • (D) plunge — CORRECT: The precise structural definition for the vertical inclination of any linear geological element.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

Structural Geometry Notation Practice

Practice Problem 22: Plunge / Trend Notation

A fold hinge line is recorded as $35^\circ \to 140^\circ$. Decode this structural measurement into its constituent plunge and trend components.

Answer:

  • Plunge: $35^\circ$ (inclined $35^\circ$ downwards from the horizontal plane).
  • Trend: $140^\circ$ (pointing towards South-East, azimuth $140^\circ$).
Structural Geology & Fault Mechanics / Question 023
Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Rock Mechanics & Continuum Deformation

Q23: Rock Mechanics: Hooke's Law of Linear Elastic Deformation

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Haakon Fossen (Structural Geology, Ch. 6, pp. 110-115); Turcotte & Schubert (Geodynamics, Ch. 3)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

23.1 Fundamental Rheological Models of Rock Deformation

In continuum mechanics, rock mechanics, and structural geology (Haakon Fossen, Structural Geology, Ch. 6, pp. 110–115; Turcotte & Schubert, Geodynamics, Ch. 3), the mechanical response of a rock mass under applied stress ($\sigma$) is described by constitutive rheological laws:

Constitutive Law Mathematical Formulation Physical Behavior & Rock Rheology
Hooke's Law (Elasticity) $\sigma = E \cdot \epsilon$ Linear elastic behavior: Strain is directly proportional to stress; instantaneous and 100% recoverable upon stress release.
Newton's Law (Viscosity) $\sigma = \eta \cdot \dot{\epsilon}$ Viscous fluid flow: Stress is proportional to strain rate; permanent non-recoverable deformation.
St. Venant (Plasticity) $\sigma = \sigma_y$ Plastic yield: Permanent deformation occurs only when stress exceeds a critical yield stress.

23.2 Generalized 3D Hooke's Law

In isotropic three-dimensional rock mechanics, Hooke's law relates stress and strain through Young's Modulus ($E$) and Poisson's Ratio ($\nu$):

$$\epsilon_x = \frac{1}{E} [\sigma_x - \nu(\sigma_y + \sigma_z)]$$ $$\epsilon_y = \frac{1}{E} [\sigma_y - \nu(\sigma_x + \sigma_z)]$$ $$\epsilon_z = \frac{1}{E} [\sigma_z - \nu(\sigma_x + \sigma_y)]$$

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q23. In elastic deformation, when strain is proportional to stress is known as :
(A) Smith's law
(B) Poisson's ratio
(C) Hooke’s law
(D) None of these
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (C)

Correct Answer: (C) Hooke’s law — In elastic deformation, the linear proportionality between stress and strain ($\sigma = E \cdot \epsilon$) is known as Hooke’s law.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Smith's law — INCORRECT: No such constitutive physical law in rock mechanics.
  • (B) Poisson's ratio — INCORRECT: Poisson's ratio is a dimensionless constant ($ u = -\epsilon_{ ext{trans}} / \epsilon_{ ext{axial}}$) measuring lateral expansion, not the proportionality law itself.
  • (C) Hooke’s law — CORRECT: Formulated by Robert Hooke in 1678 (ut tensio, sic vis), established as the foundational law of linear elasticity.
  • (D) None of these — INCORRECT.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

Rock Elastic Moduli Calculation Problem

Practice Problem 23: Young's Modulus & Elastic Shortening

A cylindrical granite core of length $L_0 = 100\text{ mm}$ with Young's Modulus $E = 50\text{ GPa}$ is subjected to a uniaxial compressive stress of $\sigma = 150\text{ MPa}$. Calculate the axial elastic strain ($\epsilon$) and change in length ($\Delta L$).

Solution:

$$\epsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E} = \frac{150 \times 10^6\text{ Pa}}{50 \times 10^9\text{ Pa}} = 0.003 = 0.3\%$$ $$\Delta L = \epsilon \cdot L_0 = 0.003 \times 100\text{ mm} = 0.3\text{ mm}$$

The granite core shortens elastically by $0.3\text{ mm}$, which will be completely recovered if the stress is released.

Q24: Fold Geometry: The Hinge Line as the Line of Maximum Curvature

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Haakon Fossen (Structural Geology, Ch. 10, pp. 214-218); Ramsay & Huber (Techniques of Modern Structural Geology, Vol. 2)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

24.1 Precise Terminology in Fold Geometry

In structural geology (Fleuty, 1964, The Description of Folds; Ramsay, 1967; Haakon Fossen, Structural Geology, Ch. 10, pp. 214–218), folded surfaces are rigorously characterized by specific mathematical lines and zones:

Fold Element Mathematical / Geometric Definition Orientation & Relationship to Topography
Hinge Line (Hinge) The locus of points of maximum curvature on a folded layer profile ($ rac{d^2y}{dx^2} = ext{max}$) Intrinsic structural property; completely independent of spatial or topographic orientation.
Fold Axis A geometric line which, when moved parallel to itself in space, generates the cylindrical fold form Direction vector of cylindrical symmetry; parallel to the hinge line in cylindrical folds.
Crest Line The line connecting the highest topographic / spatial points along a folded layer Depends on spatial orientation; coincides with the hinge line only in upright vertical folds.
Trough Line The line connecting the lowest topographic / spatial points along a folded layer Depends on spatial orientation; coincides with synclinal hinge only in upright folds.
Inflection Line The line separating opposite senses of curvature (zero curvature point, $\kappa = 0$) Separates the anticline from the syncline along the fold limb.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q24. The line of maximum curvature in a fold is known as —________.
(A) trough
(B) axis
(C) crest
(D) hinge
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (D)

Correct Answer: (D) hinge — The line of maximum curvature on a folded rock surface is mathematically and structurally designated as the hinge (or hinge line).

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) trough — INCORRECT: The trough is the line of minimum structural elevation, which diverges from the hinge in inclined/plunging folds.
  • (B) axis — INCORRECT: The fold axis is an abstract directional vector generating a cylindrical fold by parallel translation, not an actual line of maximum curvature on the layer.
  • (C) crest — INCORRECT: The crest is the line connecting the highest points on the fold, which shifts away from the hinge line in asymmetrical and inclined folds.
  • (D) hinge — CORRECT: The canonical, universal structural definition established by M.J. Fleuty (1964) and J.G. Ramsay (1967).

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

Fold Morphometrics Practice Problem

Practice Problem 24: Crest vs. Hinge in an Overturned Anticline

In an inclined or overturned anticline, do the crest line and the hinge line coincide? Explain why or why not.

Answer:

No, they do not coincide. In an inclined or overturned fold, the highest topographic point (the crest) shifts onto the upper limb, while the line of maximum mathematical curvature (the hinge) remains fixed at the structural nose of the fold. The crest and hinge only coincide in strictly upright folds with a vertical axial plane.

Structural Geology & Fault Mechanics / Question 025
Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Structural Geology & Fold Classification

Q25: Fold Classification: Parallel (Concentric) Folds & Curvature Evolution with Depth

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: John G. Ramsay (Folding & Fracturing of Rocks, 1967); Ramsay & Huber (Vol. 2, pp. 308-320); Fossen (Ch. 10, pp. 225-230)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

25.1 Ramsay's Isogon Classification of Folds

In structural geology (John G. Ramsay, 1967, Folding and Fracturing of Rocks; Ramsay & Huber, The Techniques of Modern Structural Geology, Vol. 2, pp. 308–320; Fossen, Ch. 10, pp. 225–230), folds are classified based on the behavior of dip isogons and variations in orthogonal layer thickness ($t_\alpha$):

Ramsay Fold Class Layer Thickness Condition Geometric Evolution with Depth & Structural Signatures
Class 1B: Parallel Fold (Concentric) Orthogonal thickness is constant throughout: $t_\alpha = t_0 = \text{const}$ Anticlines become sharper and more cuspidate with depth; synclines become broader and flatter with depth. Terminates downward in core space problems, decollements, and cuspate detachment faults.
Class 2: Similar Fold Axial-planar thickness is constant: $T_\alpha = T_0$; orthogonal thickness thins on limbs ($t_\alpha = t_0 \cos \alpha$) Fold profile remains identical and invariant with depth; no change in curvature or sharpness; no space problem in the core.
Class 1A Limbs thicker than hinge ($t_\alpha > t_0$) Convergent dip isogons, rare in nature.
Class 1C Limbs thinner than Class 1B but thicker than Class 2 Weakly modified buckling fold.
Class 3 Extreme limb thinning ($t_\alpha < t_0 \cos \alpha$) Divergent dip isogons, typical of incompetent layers between competent competent Class 1B beds.

25.2 Mathematical Proof of Curvature Evolution in Concentric Folds

In concentric circular folding of a multilayer with constant orthogonal bed thickness $t$:

For an anticline with outer radius of curvature $R_1$, the radius of curvature of the inner underlying layer is:

$$R_2 = R_1 - t$$

As depth increases, $R$ decreases towards zero ($R \to 0$). Because curvature is the inverse of radius ($\kappa = 1/R$), the curvature $\kappa \to \infty$, forcing the anticlinal core to become infinitely sharp, pinched, and cuspidate until space runs out at depth $z = R_1$.

Conversely, for the adjacent syncline, the center of curvature lies above ground, so going downward into depth increases the radius ($R_{\text{depth}} = R_{\text{surface}} + t$), causing curvature $\kappa \to 0$, making the syncline progressively broader, open, and flatter with depth!

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q25. A fold in which the anticlines become sharper and synclines become broader with depth is known as :
(A) Parallel fold
(B) Similar fold
(C) Recumbent fold
(D) Box fold
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (A)

Correct Answer: (A) Parallel fold — A fold in which constant layer thickness causes anticlines to become sharper and synclines to become broader with depth is strictly defined as a Parallel (or Concentric) fold (Ramsay Class 1B).

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Parallel fold — CORRECT: Constant orthogonal thickness preserves layer geometry, mathematically forcing anticlinal cores to sharpen and synclinal cores to broaden with depth.
  • (B) Similar fold — INCORRECT: In similar folds (Class 2), the fold shape and sharpness are strictly invariant and identical at all depths.
  • (C) Recumbent fold — INCORRECT: Recumbent describes a spatial orientation where the axial plane is sub-horizontal (dip $< 10^\circ$), regardless of curvature evolution with depth.
  • (D) Box fold — INCORRECT: A box fold (conjugate fold) has two distinct axial planes and a broad, flat crest.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

Structural Core Space Problem Practice

Practice Problem 25: The Space Problem at the Core of Parallel Folds

What structural features commonly develop in sedimentary basins to accommodate the severe "space problem" in the sharp core of a parallel anticline?

Answer:

Because concentric beds cannot penetrate into a negative radius of curvature, the core experiences extreme compressive jamming, accommodated by:
1. Detachment / Decollement thrusting: The competent folded stack detaches from the underlying flat basement.
2. Out-of-the-core thrust faults: Reverse faults propagate upwards out of the tight hinge.
3. Core flowage of incompetent material: Flow of ductile salt, shale, or gypsum into the anticlinal core (forming salt or shale diapirs).

Structural Geology & Fault Mechanics / Question 026
Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Structural Geology & Extensional Tectonics

Q26: Graben, Horst & Continental Rift Valley Tectonics

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Van der Pluijm & Marshak (Earth Structure, Ch. 16, pp. 412-420); Haakon Fossen (Structural Geology, 2nd Ed., Ch. 17)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

26.1 Extensional Fault Systems & Graben Geometry

In structural geology and tectonics (Van der Pluijm & Marshak, Earth Structure, 2nd Ed., Ch. 16; Haakon Fossen, Structural Geology, 2nd Ed., Ch. 17), crustal extension produces conjugate pairs of normal faults. When regional tensional stress (where maximum principal stress $\sigma_1$ is vertical and minimum principal stress $\sigma_3$ is horizontal) acts on brittle lithosphere, characteristic fault-block morphologies develop:

Morphotectonic Feature Kinematic & Geometric Definition Structural Displacement Global & Indian Examples
Graben (Rift Valley) A depressed, elongate crustal valley bounded on both flanks by inward-dipping conjugate normal faults. Downthrown central block (hanging wall of both faults) relative to flanks. East African Rift, Rhine Graben, Narmada-Tapi Rift (SONATA).
Horst An elevated, elongate crustal ridge bounded by outward-dipping normal faults. Upthrown central block (footwall of both faults) relative to flanking grabens. Vosges and Black Forest (flanking Rhine Graben), Satpura Range.
Half-Graben An asymmetric depression tilted towards a single major master listric border fault. Hanging-wall block undergoes rollover anticlinal deformation and tilt. Basin and Range Province, East African lake basins.
Fault Escarpment A steep topographic scarp formed directly by differential vertical slip on a single fault plane. Linear step in topography along a single fault trace. Wasatch fault scarp (Utah).

26.2 Continental Rifting & Lithospheric Attenuation Mechanics

Active and passive rifting mechanisms lead to lithospheric thinning ($eta$-factor, McKenzie 1978):

$$eta = rac{t_0}{t_1}$$

Where $t_0$ is initial crustal thickness and $t_1$ is thinned post-rift thickness. Subsidence of the central graben floor is accommodated initially by fault-controlled mechanical crustal stretching (syn-rift phase), followed by regional thermal cooling subsidence (post-rift sag phase).

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q26. A valley formed by the downward displacement of a fault bounded block is known as :
(A) Nappe
(B) Fault escarpment
(C) Graben
(D) All of these
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (C)

Correct Answer: (C) Graben — A valley formed by the downward displacement of a crustal block bounded on either side by normal faults is universally designated in structural geology as a Graben (or Rift Valley).

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Nappe — INCORRECT: A nappe is a massive, allochthonous rock sheet or recumbent fold that has moved tens to hundreds of kilometers horizontally along a low-angle thrust fault in a contractional orogen (e.g., Swiss Alps or Himalayas), entirely unrelated to extensional downthrown valleys.
  • (B) Fault escarpment — INCORRECT: A fault escarpment is simply the cliff-like surface slope formed by vertical offset along an individual fault plane; it is not a fault-bounded downthrown valley.
  • (C) Graben — CORRECT: From the German word for "ditch" or "trench", a graben is defined precisely as an elongate valley formed by the downward subsidence of a central block bounded by normal faults.
  • (D) All of these — INCORRECT: Erroneous combination of contractional (nappe), geomorphic (escarpment), and extensional graben terms.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

High-Yield Concept Check & Numerical Application

Practice Problem 26: Graben Subsidence from Conjugate Normal Faulting

A symmetrical continental graben is bounded by two conjugate planar normal faults each dipping at $\delta = 60^\circ$. If horizontal crustal extension produces a net heave of $H = 2.4\text{ km}$ across the basin ($1.2\text{ km}$ heave per fault), calculate the vertical structural throw (subsidence of the graben floor) accommodated by each fault.

Solution:

For a planar normal fault with dip angle $\delta$, the relationship between vertical throw ($T$) and horizontal heave ($H_f$) is:

$$T = H_f \times \tan(\delta)$$

Given $H_f = 1.2\text{ km}$ and $\delta = 60^\circ$ ($ an 60^\circ = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732$):

$$T = 1.2 \times 1.732 = 2.08\text{ km}$$

Thus, each border fault accommodates approximately $2.08\text{ km}$ of vertical graben subsidence.

Structural Geology & Fault Mechanics / Question 027
Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Structural Geology & Coordinate Geometry

Q27: Plunge of Linear Structural Features & Coordinate Geometry

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Marland P. Billings (Structural Geology, 3rd Ed., Ch. 3); Haakon Fossen (Ch. 2, pp. 24-28)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

27.1 Spatial Definition of Linear Structural Elements

In structural geology (Billings, Structural Geology, 3rd Ed., Ch. 3; Haakon Fossen, Structural Geology, Ch. 2; Van der Pluijm & Marshak, Ch. 1), the spatial orientation of any linear geological feature (fold hinge lines, mineral elongation lineations, intersection lineations, slickenlines) is defined in 3D Euclidean space by two fundamental angles:

Coordinate Element Angular Definition Measurement Plane & Reference Angular Bounds
Plunge ($\alpha$) The vertical angle between the horizontal plane and the line of maximum elongation of the feature. Measured strictly downward in the vertical plane passing through the lineation. $0^\circ \le \alpha \le 90^\circ$
Trend ($\beta$) The geographic compass bearing / azimuth of the horizontal projection of the plunging lineation. Measured clockwise from True North in the horizontal plane. $000^\circ \le \beta < 360^\circ$
Pitch / Rake ($\phi$) The angle between the linear feature and the strike line of the inclined plane on which it lies. Measured within the inclined plane containing the feature. $0^\circ \le \phi \le 90^\circ$
Dip Angle ($\delta$) The maximum angle of inclination of a planar surface measured relative to the horizontal. Measured in a vertical plane perpendicular to strike. $0^\circ \le \delta \le 90^\circ$

27.2 Stereographic Projection & Lineation Notation

A plunging lineation is recorded in standard structural notation as Plunge → Trend (e.g., $34^\circ \to 210^\circ$). The fundamental spherical trigonometry equation linking plunge ($\alpha$), pitch ($\phi$), and plane dip ($\delta$) is:

$$\sin(\alpha) = \sin(\delta) \times \sin(\phi)$$

Note on Exam Paper Nuance: In the official OPSC 2021 Question Paper, Question 27 repeats verbatim the question statement of Question 22. In both instances, the vertical angle between the horizontal plane and the axis/line of maximum elongation is strictly plunge.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q27. The vertical angle between the horizontal plane and the axis or line of maximum elongation of a feature is called ____.
(A) dip angle
(B) strike
(C) right-lateral strike slip
(D) plunge
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (D)

Correct Answer: (D) plunge — The vertical angle between the horizontal plane and the axis or line of maximum elongation of a structural feature is defined as plunge.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) dip angle — INCORRECT: Dip angle applies exclusively to planar surfaces (e.g., bedding planes, fault surfaces, foliation), representing the angle of inclination of the plane relative to the horizontal.
  • (B) strike — INCORRECT: Strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line formed by the intersection of an inclined planar feature with the horizontal plane ($000^\circ$–$360^\circ$).
  • (C) right-lateral strike slip — INCORRECT: A kinematic sense of fault motion (dextral) where the opposite block moves to the observer's right, having no angular coordinate meaning.
  • (D) plunge — CORRECT: Precisely defines the vertical inclination of a linear element measured downward from the horizontal plane.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

High-Yield Coordinate Conversion & Numerical Problem

Practice Problem 27: Pitch to Plunge Trigonometric Conversion

A mineral stretching lineation lies on a fault plane dipping at $\delta = 60^\circ$. If the pitch (rake) of the lineation measured on the fault plane is $\phi = 30^\circ$, calculate the true plunge ($\alpha$) of the lineation.

Solution:

Using the spherical kinematic relation:

$$\sin(\alpha) = \sin(\delta) \times \sin(\phi)$$ $$\sin(\alpha) = \sin(60^\circ) \times \sin(30^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1.732}{4} = 0.433$$ $$\alpha = \arcsin(0.433) \approx 25.66^\circ$$

The true plunge of the mineral lineation is approximately $25.7^\circ$.

Structural Geology & Fault Mechanics / Question 028
Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Structural Geology & Fault Mechanics

Q28: Fault Classification & Slip Kinematics (Dip-Slip vs. Strike-Slip)

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Van der Pluijm & Marshak (Ch. 16, pp. 402-408); Haakon Fossen (Ch. 8, pp. 154-160); Bangar (Ch. 8)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

28.1 Kinematic Classification of Faults Based on Net Slip Vector

In structural geology and geomechanics (Van der Pluijm & Marshak, Ch. 16; Fossen, Ch. 8; Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 8), faults are fractures along which measurable relative displacement has occurred parallel to the fracture surface. The classification depends on the orientation of the net slip vector relative to the strike and dip of the fault plane:

Fault Class Slip Vector Orientation Rake / Pitch on Fault Kinematic Sub-types
Dip-Slip Fault Movement is parallel to the dip direction of the fault surface (strictly up or down the dip). $\text{Rake } \approx 90^\circ$ Normal Fault (hanging wall moves down; extension)
Reverse / Thrust Fault (hanging wall moves up; contraction)
Strike-Slip Fault (Transcurrent / Wrench) Movement is parallel to the horizontal strike line of the fault plane. $\text{Rake } \approx 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$ Sinistral (left-lateral)
Dextral (right-lateral)
Oblique-Slip Fault Movement has significant components of both strike-slip and dip-slip. Intermediate rake ($10^\circ < \phi < 80^\circ$) Transtensional (normal + strike-slip)
Transpressional (reverse + strike-slip)
Step Fault A geometric series of parallel normal faults stepping down in the same direction. Dip-slip arrangement Structural terrace / staircase graben boundary

28.2 Components of Fault Displacement Vector

In 3D Cartesian coordinates on the fault surface, net slip ($S_{\text{net}}$) is resolved into:

$$S_{\text{net}}^2 = S_{\text{strike}}^2 + S_{\text{dip}}^2$$

Where pure dip-slip occurs, $S_{\text{strike}} = 0$ and $S_{\text{net}} = S_{\text{dip}}$. The vertical component of dip slip is termed the throw ($T = S_{\text{dip}} \sin\delta$), and the horizontal component perpendicular to strike is termed the heave ($H = S_{\text{dip}} \cos\delta$).

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q28. A fault in which the movement is parallel to the dip of the fault is called :
(A) Step fault
(B) Dip-slip fault
(C) Strike-slip fault
(D) None of these
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (B)

Correct Answer: (B) Dip-slip fault — A fault in which the relative movement of the blocks is parallel to the dip of the fault surface is unequivocally designated as a Dip-slip fault.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Step fault — INCORRECT: Step faulting refers to a structural arrangement or pattern of multiple parallel faults downthrown in steps in the same direction, not the kinematic definition of motion along the dip.
  • (B) Dip-slip fault — CORRECT: Standard textbook definition: relative movement parallel to the true dip direction of the fault surface. Includes both normal and reverse/thrust faults.
  • (C) Strike-slip fault — INCORRECT: Motion is parallel to the horizontal strike line of the fault plane, with zero or negligible vertical dip-slip displacement.
  • (D) None of these — INCORRECT: Option (B) is the universally recognized correct term.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

High-Yield Fault Kinematics & Practice Problem

Practice Problem 28: Resolving Net Slip and Rake Angle

A slickensided fault plane has an observed strike-slip component of $S_s = 60\text{ m}$ and a dip-slip component of $S_d = 80\text{ m}$. Calculate the net slip ($S_{\text{net}}$) and the rake angle ($\phi$) of the movement vector on the fault surface.

Solution:

1. The net slip magnitude is given by the Pythagorean theorem on the fault plane:

$$S_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{S_s^2 + S_d^2} = \sqrt{60^2 + 80^2} = \sqrt{3600 + 6400} = \sqrt{10000} = 100\text{ m}$$

2. The rake angle ($\phi$) measured from the strike line is:

$$\tan(\phi) = \frac{S_d}{S_s} = \frac{80}{60} = 1.3333$$ $$\phi = \arctan(1.3333) \approx 53.13^\circ$$

Because the rake angle is $53.1^\circ$, this is classified as an oblique-slip fault (transpressional or transtensional depending on whether $S_d$ is reverse or normal).

Structural Geology & Fault Mechanics / Question 029
Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Sedimentology & Stratigraphy

Q29: Stratigraphic Unconformities: Disconformity vs. Paraconformity

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, 5th Ed., Ch. 14, pp. 498-504); Dunbar & Rodgers (1957)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

29.1 Boggs Classification of Stratigraphic Unconformities

In stratigraphy and physical geology (Sam Boggs Jr., Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, 5th Ed., Ch. 14; Dunbar & Rodgers, 1957; Bangar, Ch. 9), an unconformity is a substantial break or gap in the geologic rock record resulting from a period of non-deposition and/or erosion. The four canonical types are distinguished by geometric relationships and basement lithology:

Unconformity Type Geometric Bedding Relation Physical Boundary Characteristics Diagnostic Evidence
Disconformity Beds above and below the unconformity are strictly parallel ($S_1 \parallel S_2$). Visible, irregular, undulating erosional surface (paleo-channels, paleosols, karst relief, basal gravels). Identified physically by erosional relief despite parallel structural attitude.
Paraconformity Beds above and below are parallel. Completely flat, planar contact with no visible erosional relief; looks like a normal bedding plane. Can only be identified biostratigraphically (missing biozones) or chronostratigraphically.
Angular Unconformity Younger strata overlie tilted, folded, or deformed older strata at an angular discordance. Structural discordance where underlying beds are truncated by younger horizontal strata. Classic Hutton's unconformity at Siccar Point; clear tectonic tilting prior to erosion.
Nonconformity Sedimentary strata overlie unstratified, eroded plutonic igneous (granite) or metamorphic basement rocks. Erosional contact on crystalline basement; lacks contact metamorphism in upper strata. Great Eparchean Unconformity (e.g., Cuddapah or Vindhyan over Archean granite/gneiss).

29.2 Chronostratigraphic Significance: The Hiatus & Vacuity

The time interval represented by an unconformity is termed the hiatus, which comprises the erosional vacuity (time represented by eroded rocks) plus the non-depositional interval. In a disconformity, the parallelism indicates epeirogenic regional uplift and emergence without crustal orogenic tilting.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q29. A type of unconformity in which the beds above and below are parallel is termed as :
(A) Parallel unconformity
(B) Discontinuity
(C) Non-conformity
(D) Disconformity
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (D)

Correct Answer: (D) Disconformity — An unconformity in which the sedimentary beds above and below are structurally parallel and separated by a visible erosional boundary is designated as a Disconformity.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Parallel unconformity — INCORRECT: Informal or non-standard descriptive phrase; the rigorous academic term standardized by Dunbar & Rodgers and Sam Boggs Jr. is disconformity.
  • (B) Discontinuity — INCORRECT: Generic mechanical term representing any break or joint plane in a rock mass (used in engineering rock mechanics, e.g., ISRM standards), not a specific stratigraphic unconformity.
  • (C) Non-conformity — INCORRECT: A nonconformity specifically requires that sedimentary strata overlie older eroded plutonic igneous or metamorphic crystalline rocks, not stratified sedimentary beds.
  • (D) Disconformity — CORRECT: The exact, formal stratigraphic term for an erosional gap between parallel sedimentary strata.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

High-Yield Stratigraphic Synthesis & Practice Problem

Practice Problem 29: Distinguishing Disconformity from Paraconformity

Two horizontal limestone units are in direct contact. Unit A (below) contains Lower Devonian spiriferid brachiopods, while Unit B (above) contains Upper Mississippian goniatites. The contact surface shows $1.5\text{ m}$ deep incised paleo-karst potholes filled with chert lag gravel. Classify this unconformity and estimate the missing temporal interval.

Solution:

1. Classification: Because the beds above and below are structurally parallel (horizontal), and the contact exhibits prominent, undulating erosional topography (incised paleokarst potholes and chert lag gravels), the contact is definitively a Disconformity (if the contact were a perfectly flat, featureless bedding plane, it would be a paraconformity).

2. Temporal Hiatus: The hiatus spans the Middle Devonian, Late Devonian, and Early Mississippian epochs (approximately $\sim 393\text{ Ma}$ to $\sim 330\text{ Ma} = \approx 63\text{ million years}$ of missing rock record).

GEO - 2/21 • Surveying & Field Geology

Q30: Cartographic Representative Fraction (RF) & Geological Map Scaling

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Robert R. Compton (Manual of Field Geology); K.M. Bangar (Ch. 1, pp. 12-16)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

30.1 Principles of Representative Fraction (RF) in Topographic & Geological Maps

In cartography, surveying, and field geology (Compton, Manual of Field Geology; Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 1), the scale of a map defines the proportional ratio between a distance measured on the map and the corresponding horizontal distance measured on the ground:

$$\text{Scale} = \frac{\text{Map Distance } (d_m)}{\text{Ground Distance } (D_g)}$$

When expressed as a Representative Fraction (RF):

$$\text{RF} = \frac{1}{M}$$

Where $M$ is the scale denominator (scale factor). Crucially, RF is a dimensionless ratio; both $d_m$ and $D_g$ must be expressed in identical metric units:

$$D_g = d_m \times M$$

30.2 Metric Unit Scaling Conversions

Standard Survey of India (SOI) Scale RF Equivalent Ground Distance for $1\text{ cm}$ on Map Application Domain
$1\text{ cm} = 2.5\text{ km}$ $1 : 250,000$ $2,500\text{ m}$ ($2.5\text{ km}$) Regional tectonic synoptic sheets
$1\text{ cm} = 500\text{ m}$ $1 : 50,000$ $500\text{ m}$ ($0.5\text{ km}$) Standard SOI Toposheets
$1\text{ cm} = 250\text{ m}$ $1 : 25,000$ $250\text{ m}$ High-resolution mineral exploration & engineering geology maps
$1\text{ cm} = 100\text{ m}$ $1 : 10,000$ $100\text{ m}$ Detailed mine working & pit design plans

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q30. The distance between two points on a 1: 25,000 map is 1.5 cm than the true distance between these points on the field will be :
(A) 375 m
(B) 3750 km
(C) 3750 cm
(D) 37500 mm
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (A)

Correct Answer: (A) 375 m — On a $1:25,000$ scale map, $1.5\text{ cm}$ measured on the map corresponds exactly to $1.5 \times 25,000 = 37,500\text{ cm} = \mathbf{375\text{ m}}$ on the ground.

Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

1. Identify the Representative Fraction: $\text{RF} = 1 : 25,000$. This implies $1\text{ unit on map} = 25,000\text{ units on ground}$.

2. Calculate field ground distance in centimeters:

$$D_g = d_m \times 25,000 = 1.5\text{ cm} \times 25,000 = 37,500\text{ cm}$$

3. Convert centimeters to meters ($1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm}$):

$$D_g = \frac{37,500\text{ cm}}{100\text{ cm/m}} = \mathbf{375\text{ m}}$$

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) 375 m — CORRECT: Exact mathematical conversion: $37,500\text{ cm} = 375\text{ m}$.
  • (B) 3750 km — INCORRECT: Catastrophic unit conversion error by a factor of $10,000$ (representing $3,750,000\text{ m}$).
  • (C) 3750 cm — INCORRECT: Off by an order of magnitude (would correspond to an RF of $1:2,500$).
  • (D) 37500 mm — INCORRECT: $37,500\text{ mm} = 37.5\text{ m}$, which is off by a factor of 10.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

Advanced Cartographic Scale Problems

Practice Problem 30: Areal Scale & Open-Pit Mine Conversion

An open-pit iron ore lease boundary covers an area of $8.0\text{ cm}^2$ on a $1:25,000$ geological map. What is the actual ground surface area of the mining lease in square kilometers ($ ext{km}^2$) and in hectares ($ ext{ha}$)?

Solution:

1. The areal scale is the square of the linear scale factor:

$$\text{Area Ground} = \text{Area Map} \times M^2$$ $$A_g = 8.0\text{ cm}^2 \times (25,000)^2 = 8.0 \times 625,000,000\text{ cm}^2 = 5,000,000,000\text{ cm}^2$$

2. Convert to square meters ($1\text{ m}^2 = 10,000\text{ cm}^2$):

$$A_g = \frac{5,000,000,000}{10,000} = 500,000\text{ m}^2$$

3. Convert to square kilometers ($1\text{ km}^2 = 1,000,000\text{ m}^2$) and hectares ($1\text{ ha} = 10,000\text{ m}^2$):

$$A_g = \frac{500,000}{1,000,000} = \mathbf{0.50\text{ km}^2} = \mathbf{50.0\text{ hectares}}$$

Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Structural Geology & Mining

Q31: Apparent Dip vs. True Dip Trigonometric Nomography

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: M.P. Billings (Structural Geology, Appendix B); Haakon Fossen (Ch. 2, pp. 28-30)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

31.1 Geometric Derivation of Apparent Dip

In structural geology and underground mining (Billings, Structural Geology, Appendix B; Fossen, Ch. 2; Van der Pluijm & Marshak, Ch. 1), true dip ($\delta$) is the maximum angle of inclination of a planar structure measured perpendicular to the strike line. In any other vertical cross-section oriented oblique to the true dip direction, the observed inclination is the apparent dip ($\delta'$), which is always less than the true dip:

$$\delta' < \delta \quad (\text{for any angle } \alpha > 0^\circ)$$

The universal trigonometric formula relating true dip ($\delta$), apparent dip ($\delta'$), and the angular deviation between their azimuth directions ($\alpha$) is:

$$\mathbf{\tan(\delta') = \tan(\delta) \times \cos(\alpha)}$$

Where:

  • $\delta$ = True dip angle (measured in the direction of true dip).
  • $\delta'$ = Apparent dip angle (measured along an oblique vertical section).
  • $\alpha = |\text{Azimuth}_{\text{true dip}} - \text{Azimuth}_{\text{apparent dip}}|$ = Horizontal angle between the true dip bearing and the apparent dip bearing.

31.2 Critical Limiting Cases

Bearing of Oblique Section Relative to True Dip Angular Offset ($\alpha$) $\cos(\alpha)$ Resulting Apparent Dip ($\delta'$)
Parallel to True Dip Direction $\alpha = 0^\circ$ $\cos(0^\circ) = 1.0$ $\tan\delta' = \tan\delta \implies \mathbf{\delta' = \delta}$ (Maximum inclination)
Oblique to True Dip Direction ($0^\circ < \alpha < 90^\circ$) e.g. $\alpha = 25^\circ$ $\cos(25^\circ) \approx 0.906$ $\mathbf{\delta' < \delta}$ (Intermediate apparent dip)
Parallel to Strike Direction $\alpha = 90^\circ$ $\cos(90^\circ) = 0.0$ $\tan\delta' = 0 \implies \mathbf{\delta' = 0^\circ}$ (Horizontal line)

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q31. A sulphide vein dips 50° toward N45°W. Its apparent dip toward of N20°W will be around _____.
(A) 65°
(B) 60°
(C) 0°
(D) 45°
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (D)

Correct Answer: (D) 45° — Applying the apparent dip equation for a vein dipping $\delta = 50^\circ$ toward $\text{N}45^\circ\text{W}$ when viewed toward $\text{N}20^\circ\text{W}$ gives an angular offset $\alpha = 25^\circ$, yielding an apparent dip of $\delta' \approx 47.2^\circ \approx \mathbf{45^\circ}$.

Step-by-Step Mathematical Calculation

1. Identify the given parameters:

  • True dip angle: $\delta = 50^\circ$
  • True dip direction: $\text{N}45^\circ\text{W}$ ($315^\circ$ azimuth)
  • Apparent dip direction: $\text{N}20^\circ\text{W}$ ($340^\circ$ azimuth)

2. Calculate horizontal angular difference $\alpha$:

$$\alpha = |45^\circ - 20^\circ| = 25^\circ$$

3. Apply the nomographic apparent dip formula:

$$\tan(\delta') = \tan(50^\circ) \times \cos(25^\circ)$$

Using standard trigonometric tables: $\tan(50^\circ) = 1.19175$, and $\cos(25^\circ) = 0.90631$:

$$\tan(\delta') = 1.19175 \times 0.90631 = 1.08009$$ $$\delta' = \arctan(1.08009) = 47.20^\circ$$

4. Match with exam options: Among the choices ($65^\circ, 60^\circ, 0^\circ, 45^\circ$), the only physically possible and closest answer is 45° (since apparent dip must be less than true dip $50^\circ$, options A and B are impossible, while $0^\circ$ is only along strike).

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) 65° — IMPOSSIBLE: Violates the fundamental geometric law of structural geology: apparent dip can NEVER exceed true dip ($\delta' \le \delta$). A $50^\circ$ vein cannot have an apparent dip of $65^\circ$.
  • (B) 60° — IMPOSSIBLE: Exceeds true dip ($60^\circ > 50^\circ$); physically impossible.
  • (C) 0° — INCORRECT: Apparent dip is only $0^\circ$ when viewed strictly parallel to strike (which would be $\text{N}45^\circ\text{E}$ or $\text{S}45^\circ\text{W}$), not $\text{N}20^\circ\text{W}$.
  • (D) 45° — CORRECT: The only mathematically sound option consistent with $\delta' = 47.2^\circ \approx 45^\circ$ and satisfying $\delta' < 50^\circ$.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

High-Yield Mining Nomogram Problem

Practice Problem 31: Apparent Dip for Underground Cross-Cut Tunnel

A coal seam has a true dip of $35^\circ$ due South ($180^\circ$). An underground haulage drift is driven along a bearing of $\text{S}60^\circ\text{W}$ ($240^\circ$). Calculate the apparent gradient (slope angle) of the coal seam along the wall of this haulage drift.

Solution:

1. The angular difference between true dip direction ($180^\circ$) and drift bearing ($240^\circ$) is:

$$\alpha = 240^\circ - 180^\circ = 60^\circ$$

2. Calculate apparent dip using $\tan(\delta') = \tan(\delta) \cos(\alpha)$:

$$\tan(\delta') = \tan(35^\circ) \times \cos(60^\circ) = 0.7002 \times 0.5000 = 0.3501$$ $$\delta' = \arctan(0.3501) \approx 19.29^\circ$$

The seam appears to dip at approximately $19.3^\circ$ along the haulage drift.

Q32: Himalayan Orogenic Wedge Tectonics (Contractional Folds & Thrust Faults)

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: K.S. Valdiya (The Making of India, Ch. 5); Augusto Gansser (Geology of the Himalayas, 1964)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

32.1 Tectonic Architecture of the India-Asia Collisional Orogen

In global tectonics and Indian geology (K.S. Valdiya, The Making of India: Geodynamic Evolution, Ch. 5; Gansser, 1964; Ramakrishnan & Vaidyanadhan, Geology of India, Vol. 2, Ch. 29), the Himalayan mountain belt represents the classic, archetypal active continental collision zone (Himalayan-Tibetan orogen). Driven by the ongoing northward indentation of the Indian plate into Eurasia at $\sim 40 - 50\text{ mm/yr}$, crustal shortening is accommodated by a massive foreland-propagating fold-and-thrust belt:

Major Tectonic Boundary / Unit Structural Architecture Dominant Deformational Regime Lithotectonic Association
Main Central Thrust (MCT) Ductile, high-angle shear zone transitioning into crustal ramp Contractional Thrusting + Overturned Folds High-grade Higher Himalayan Crystalline core over Lesser Himalaya.
Main Boundary Thrust (MBT) Regional northward-dipping low-angle thrust fault Contractional Thrusting + Nappes Lesser Himalayan metasediments thrust over the Siwaliks.
Main Frontal Thrust (MFT / HFT) Active southernmost frontal reverse fault Blind thrusts, Fault-bend folds, Fault-propagation folds Siwalik molasse thrust over active Indo-Gangetic alluvium.
Sub-Himalayan Siwalik Belt Fold-thrust wedge Asymmetrical anticlines, synclines, & imbricate thrusts Neogene-Quaternary foreland synorogenic sediments.

32.2 Why Normal Faults are Minor and Restricted

While the South Tibetan Detachment System (STDS) at the crest of the Higher Himalaya exhibits localized orogen-parallel extension due to gravitational collapse of over-thickened crust, the overwhelming bulk of the deformed rocks across the length and breadth of the Himalayan belt forms folds and reverse/thrust faults under regional horizontal compression ($\sigma_1$ horizontal, $\sigma_3$ vertical).

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q32. Rocks are deformed in the Himalayan mountain belt commonly forms which deformational structures ?
(A) Normal and reverse faults
(B) Folds and reverse faults
(C) Recumbent folds and normal faults
(D) All of these
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (B)

Correct Answer: (B) Folds and reverse faults — Regional crustal shortening in the Himalayan contractional collision orogen produces predominantly folds and reverse (thrust) faults throughout the belt.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Normal and reverse faults — INCORRECT: Normal faults characterize extensional tectonic environments (rifts), whereas the Himalayas are an active compressional convergent orogen.
  • (B) Folds and reverse faults — CORRECT: The hallmark deformational structures of collisional mountain belts (MCT, MBT, MFT, and associated Siwalik and Lesser Himalayan fold-thrust nappes) are compressive folds and reverse/thrust faults.
  • (C) Recumbent folds and normal faults — INCORRECT: While recumbent folds occur locally in the crystalline nappes, normal faults are not the characteristic widespread deformation structure of the range.
  • (D) All of these — INCORRECT: Normal faults are not a primary characteristic of the general Himalayan deformation belt.

Tectonic Setting Stress Regime Dominant Structures Representative Global Example

Continental Rifting $\sigma_1$ vertical, $\sigma_3$ horizontal Normal Faults, Grabens, Tilted Blocks East African Rift, Basin & Range

Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Structural Geology & Fold Classification

Q33: Recumbent Fold Geometry & Axial Surface Inclination

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: M.J. Fleuty (The Description of Folds, 1964); Haakon Fossen (Ch. 11, pp. 240-244)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

33.1 Fleuty's (1964) Classification of Folds by Axial Surface Dip

In structural geology (M.J. Fleuty, 1964, The Description of Folds; Haakon Fossen, Structural Geology, Ch. 11; Billings, Ch. 4; Bangar, Ch. 7), folds are rigorously categorized according to the inclination (dip angle $\delta_{\text{ap}}$) of their axial surface (axial plane):

Fold Category Dip of Axial Surface ($\delta_{\text{ap}}$) Limb Attitude & Structural Symmetry Geotectonic Significance
Upright Fold $\delta_{\text{ap}} = 80^\circ - 90^\circ$ (Vertical to Sub-vertical) Limbs dip symmetrically in opposite directions at equal angles. Mild to moderate horizontal compression.
Steeply Inclined Fold $\delta_{\text{ap}} = 60^\circ - 80^\circ$ Asymmetrical limbs dipping in opposite directions. Progressive asymmetric shear.
Moderately Inclined Fold $\delta_{\text{ap}} = 30^\circ - 60^\circ$ Asymmetrical limbs. Oblique contractional shortening.
Gently Inclined Fold $\delta_{\text{ap}} = 10^\circ - 30^\circ$ One limb normal, one limb overturned. Intense overthrust shear strain.
Recumbent Fold $\mathbf{\delta_{\text{ap}} = 0^\circ - 10^\circ}$ (Sub-horizontal to Horizontal, $\approx 0^\circ$) Axial plane is horizontal; the lower limb is completely overturned and inverted. Extreme ductile shear nappe transport in metamorphic cores.

33.2 Anatomy of a Recumbent Fold

In a true recumbent fold, the fold lies essentially on its side. It consists of:

  • Upper Normal Limb (Digit): Strata are in normal stratigraphic superposition (younger beds over older beds).
  • Hinge Zone (Closure): Point of maximum curvature where the axial surface trace is sub-horizontal.
  • Lower Inverted Limb (Flank): Strata are completely overturned (inverted, upside down; older beds over younger beds), often subjected to extreme ductile attenuation and shearing, eventually detaching along thrusts to generate nappes.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q33. In a recumbent fold, the axial plane dips about _____.
(A) 45°
(B) 90°
(C) 60°
(D) 0°
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (D)

Correct Answer: (D) 0° — In a recumbent fold, the defining structural criterion is that the axial plane dips sub-horizontally, essentially at 0° ($\le 10^\circ$).

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) 45° — INCORRECT: An axial plane dipping at $45^\circ$ defines an inclined fold, not a recumbent fold.
  • (B) 90° — INCORRECT: An axial plane dipping at $90^\circ$ defines an upright (vertical) fold.
  • (C) 60° — INCORRECT: An axial plane dipping at $60^\circ$ defines a steeply inclined fold.
  • (D) 0° — CORRECT: By universal academic definition (Fleuty 1964; Fossen; Billings), a recumbent fold is a fold whose axial surface is horizontal to sub-horizontal (dip $\approx 0^\circ$).

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

High-Yield Fold Anatomy Problem

Practice Problem 33: Identifying Facing and Vergence in Recumbent Nappes

A geologist in the Lesser Himalayan Almora Nappe observes graded turbidite sandstone beds on the lower limb of a large recumbent fold whose axial surface dips at $4^\circ\text{ North}$. The coarse pebbles are found at the stratigraphic top of each bed while fine silts are at the bottom. What is the facing direction and structural status of this limb?

Solution:

1. In graded bedding, normal younging direction (facing) requires coarse grains at the bottom grading upward to fine grains at the top. Here, coarse pebbles are at the top, indicating that the strata are stratigraphically inverted (overturned).

2. In a recumbent fold with an axial surface dip of $4^\circ \approx 0^\circ$, the lower limb is the inverted / overturned limb. Facing is directed downward, confirming classic recumbent nappe kinematics.

Structural Geology & Fault Mechanics / Question 034
Standalone View
GEO - 2/21 • Structural Geology & Crustal Rheology

Q34: Crustal Rheology & Brittle vs. Ductile Deformation Regimes

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Van der Pluijm & Marshak (Ch. 7, pp. 148-156); J. Byerlee (Friction of Rocks, 1978); R.H. Sibson (1977)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

34.1 Byerlee's Law & Frictional Failure in the Upper Crust

In structural geology, rock mechanics, and lithospheric dynamics (Byerlee, 1978; Sibson, 1977; Van der Pluijm & Marshak, Ch. 7; Fossen, Ch. 6), the deformation behavior of lithospheric rocks is governed by confining pressure ($P$), temperature ($T$), fluid pressure ($P_f$), and strain rate ($\dot{\varepsilon}$):

Crustal Domain P-T Conditions & Typical Depth Dominant Deformation Mechanism Characteristic Microstructures & Structures
Upper Crust Low Temperature ($T < 300^\circ\text{C}$) & Low Confining Pressure ($P < 300\text{ MPa}$); Depth: $0 - 10\text{–}15\text{ km}$ Brittle Process (Frictional Cataclasis & Fracture) Joints, Faults, Microcracking, Frictional Sliding (Byerlee's Law), Cataclasites, Fault Gouge, Pseudotachylytes.
Brittle-Ductile Transition (BDT) $T \approx 300^\circ - 350^\circ\text{C}$, Depth $\sim 10 - 15\text{ km}$ in quartz-bearing continental crust Semi-brittle / Transitional Greenschist facies transition; onset of quartz crystal plasticity; peak crustal shear strength.
Middle to Lower Crust High Temperature ($T > 350^\circ - 500^\circ\text{C}$) & High Pressure; Depth $> 15\text{ km}$ Ductile / Plastic Process (Viscous Crystal Plasticity) Dislocation creep, dynamic recrystallization, mylonites, solid-state flow, ductile folds.

34.2 Byerlee's Frictional Law

In the brittle upper crust, rock shear strength ($\tau$) is pressure-dependent but almost entirely independent of rock type and temperature (Byerlee's Law):

$$\tau = 0.85 \sigma_n \quad (\text{for } \sigma_n < 200\text{ MPa})$$ $$\tau = 50\text{ MPa} + 0.6 \sigma_n \quad (\text{for } \sigma_n > 200\text{ MPa})$$

Because rocks fail along discrete fractures and slip planes under these low P-T conditions before any significant crystal-plastic flow can occur, deformation is overwhelmingly brittle.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q34. In the upper crust where The P and T condition is relatively low, the deformational process dominates is :
(A) Brittle process
(B) Ductile-brittle process
(C) Plastic deformation
(D) Both (A) and (B) are true
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (A)

Correct Answer: (A) Brittle process — In the upper crust where confining pressure and temperature are relatively low, deformation is dominated by brittle processes (fracturing, jointing, cataclasis, and faulting).

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Brittle process — CORRECT: Low temperature ($< 300^\circ\text{C}$) and low confining pressure in the upper $10\text{–}15\text{ km}$ prevent crystal-plastic flow, restricting deformation to elastic strain followed by brittle frictional failure.
  • (B) Ductile-brittle process — INCORRECT: Ductile-brittle behavior is restricted to the narrow transitional zone (BDT) at mid-crustal depths ($10\text{–}15\text{ km}$), not the general low P-T upper crust.
  • (C) Plastic deformation — INCORRECT: True plastic deformation (dislocation creep, diffusion flow) requires elevated temperatures ($T > 300^\circ\text{–}500^\circ\text{C}$) occurring exclusively in the middle and lower crust or mantle.
  • (D) Both (A) and (B) are true — INCORRECT: Brittle deformation is the singular dominant mechanism governing the upper crust.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

Crustal Rheology & Strength Envelope Problem

Practice Problem 34: Calculating Brittle Failure Stress at 5 km Depth

Assuming an average upper continental crust density of $\rho = 2700\text{ kg/m}^3$ and hydrostatic pore water pressure with rock internal friction coefficient $\mu = 0.85$, calculate the vertical lithostatic stress ($\sigma_v$) at a depth of $z = 5.0\text{ km}$ ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$).

Solution:

1. The vertical overburden lithostatic stress is:

$$\sigma_v = \rho g z = 2700\text{ kg/m}^3 \times 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 \times 5000\text{ m} = 132,300,000\text{ Pa} = 132.3\text{ MPa}$$

2. Hydrostatic pore fluid pressure at $5\text{ km}$ ($\rho_w = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3$):

$$P_f = \rho_w g z = 1000 \times 9.8 \times 5000 = 49.0\text{ MPa}$$

3. Effective normal stress:

$$\sigma_v' = \sigma_v - P_f = 132.3 - 49.0 = 83.3\text{ MPa}$$

Under Byerlee's law, shear stress required to cause fault slip is $\tau = 0.85 \times 83.3 \approx 70.8\text{ MPa}$. This frictional stress threshold dictates earthquake faulting throughout the brittle seismogenic zone.

Q35: Anderson's Dynamic Theory of Faulting & Normal Fault Angles

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: E.M. Anderson (The Dynamics of Faulting, 1905, 1951); Haakon Fossen (Ch. 8, pp. 165-170)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

35.1 Anderson's (1905, 1951) Dynamic Theory of Faulting

In structural geology and geomechanics (E.M. Anderson, 1905, 1951, The Dynamics of Faulting; Fossen, Ch. 8; Van der Pluijm & Marshak, Ch. 16), the Earth's surface is a free boundary contact with the atmosphere, meaning it can support no shear stress. Consequently, one of the three principal stress axes must be vertical, and the other two must lie in the horizontal plane:

Fault Regime Principal Stress Orientation Angle to $\sigma_1$ Theoretical Dip Angle (to Horizontal) Angle to Vertical
Normal Fault $\sigma_1$ is Vertical
$\sigma_2, \sigma_3$ are Horizontal		 $\theta = 45^\circ - \frac{\phi}{2}$ from $\sigma_1$ $\delta = 45^\circ + \frac{\phi}{2} \approx \mathbf{60^\circ}$ to horizontal $\mathbf{30^\circ}$ to vertical
Thrust / Reverse Fault $\sigma_3$ is Vertical
$\sigma_1, \sigma_2$ are Horizontal		 $\theta = 45^\circ - \frac{\phi}{2}$ from $\sigma_1$ $\delta = 45^\circ - \frac{\phi}{2} \approx \mathbf{30^\circ}$ to horizontal $60^\circ$ to vertical
Strike-Slip Fault $\sigma_2$ is Vertical
$\sigma_1, \sigma_3$ are Horizontal		 $\theta = 45^\circ - \frac{\phi}{2}$ from $\sigma_1$ $\delta = 90^\circ$ (Vertical plane) $0^\circ$ to vertical

35.2 Mohr-Coulomb Criterion for Normal Fault Dip

According to the Coulomb failure criterion, conjugate shear fractures form at an angle $\theta$ to the maximum principal compressive stress ($\sigma_1$):

$$\theta = 45^\circ - \frac{\phi}{2}$$

For typical lithospheric crustal rocks, the internal friction angle is $\phi \approx 30^\circ$. Therefore:

$$\theta = 45^\circ - \frac{30^\circ}{2} = 45^\circ - 15^\circ = 30^\circ \quad (\text{angle with vertical } \sigma_1)$$

Thus, normal faults dip at an angle of $60^\circ$ to the horizontal and $30^\circ$ to the vertical. The statement claiming that the most common angle of normal faults is 45° to vertical is therefore unequivocally FALSE.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q35. Most common angle of normal faults is 45° to vertical.
(A) False
(B) True
(C) Can be true or false
(D) None of these
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (A)

Correct Answer: (A) False — The statement "Most common angle of normal faults is 45° to vertical" is False. By Anderson's fault theory and empirical global measurements, normal faults characteristically dip at $\approx 60^\circ$ to the horizontal (i.e. $\approx 30^\circ$ to the vertical).

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) False — CORRECT: Based on Mohr-Coulomb failure ($\phi pprox 30^\circ$), shear fractures form at $30^\circ$ to $\sigma_1$. Since $\sigma_1$ is vertical in normal fault regimes, the angle to vertical is $\mathbf{30^\circ}$ (dip is $60^\circ$ to horizontal), making the $45^\circ$ claim categorically false.
  • (B) True — INCORRECT: A $45^\circ$ angle would only occur in a perfectly frictionless hypothetical material ($\phi = 0^\circ$), which does not exist in crustal rocks.
  • (C) Can be true or false — INCORRECT: Standard mechanical laws provide a precise, verifiable answer.
  • (D) None of these — INCORRECT.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

Andersonian Stress State Practice Problem

Practice Problem 35: Calculating Normal Fault Dip from Friction Angle

Triaxial compressive laboratory testing on a granite core yields an internal friction angle of $\phi = 34^\circ$. In a tectonic extensional basin where this granite undergoes Andersonian normal faulting, what will be: (a) the dip angle of the normal fault relative to the horizontal, and (b) the inclination angle of the fault plane relative to the vertical?

Solution:

1. Angle with maximum compressive stress ($\sigma_1$, which is vertical):

$$\theta_v = 45^\circ - \frac{\phi}{2} = 45^\circ - \frac{34^\circ}{2} = 45^\circ - 17^\circ = \mathbf{28^\circ\text{ to the vertical}}$$

2. Dip angle relative to the horizontal ground surface:

$$\delta = 90^\circ - \theta_v = 45^\circ + \frac{\phi}{2} = 45^\circ + 17^\circ = \mathbf{62^\circ\text{ to the horizontal}}$$

This confirms that normal faults are steep ($60^\circ ext{–}65^\circ$ to horizontal, $25^\circ ext{–}30^\circ$ to vertical), never $45^\circ$.

Q36: Indian Peninsular Drainage & Rift Valleys (SONATA vs. Shield Rivers)

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: D.N. Wadia (Geology of India); Ramakrishnan & Vaidyanadhan (Vol. 2, Ch. 21); B.P. Radhakrishna (1993)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

36.1 Tectonic Geomorphology of Indian Peninsular River Systems

In Indian geomorphology and stratigraphy (D.N. Wadia, Geology of India; Ramakrishnan & Vaidyanadhan, Geology of India, Vol. 2; Radhakrishna, 1993), the Indian peninsular drainage system is divided into two radically distinct tectonic categories:

River System Flow Direction & Drainage Basin Tectonic Control & Geomorphic Setting Rift Valley Status
Narmada River Flows Westward into Gulf of Khambhat (Arabian Sea) Occupies the ancient, active SONATA (Son-Narmada-Tapi) mega-rift graben between the Vindhyan Horst (north) and Satpura Horst (south). CLASSIC RIFT VALLEY (Graben)
Tapi (Tapti) River Flows Westward into Arabian Sea Flows parallel to Narmada in the southern graben of the Satpura horst fault system. CLASSIC RIFT VALLEY (Graben)
Mahi River Flows Westward/Southwestward into Gulf of Khambhat Occupies the Cambay-Gujarat structural graben/extensional basin margin. RIFT / EXTENSIONAL TROUGH
Damodar River Flows Eastward Occupies the Gondwana fault-bounded graben trough. GONDWANA RIFT BASIN
Krishna River Flows Eastward into Bay of Bengal Originates at Mahabaleshwar (Western Ghats) and flows across the gently east-tilted peninsular crystalline/basaltic shield plateau; governed strictly by regional topographic slope. NOT A RIFT VALLEY (Consequent Shield River)

36.2 The Anomaly of Westward-Flowing Peninsular Rivers

Most Peninsular Indian rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery, Mahanadi) flow east-southeast into the Bay of Bengal because the entire Indian shield underwent an easterly regional tilt during Cretaceous-Tertiary rifting of the western continental margin. The only major rivers that flow westward against this regional shield tilt are the Narmada and Tapi, precisely because they are structural prisoners confined within deep, fault-bounded tectonic rift valleys (grabens).

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q36. Which river is not flowing through a Rift valley ?
(A) Mahi
(B) Narmada
(C) Krishna
(D) Tungabhadra
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (C)

Correct Answer: (C) Krishna — The Krishna River does not flow through a rift valley; it is a major east-flowing consequent river flowing across the tilted peninsular cratonic shield into the Bay of Bengal.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Mahi — INCORRECT: The Mahi river flows southwestward along the extension-controlled Cambay graben basin.
  • (B) Narmada — INCORRECT: The Narmada is India's most celebrated, prototypical example of a river flowing through a tectonic rift valley (the Son-Narmada lineament graben).
  • (C) Krishna — CORRECT: Originates at Mahabaleshwar in the Western Ghats and traverses the Deccan plateau shield to form a vast delta on the eastern Coromandel coast; it does not occupy a structural rift valley.
  • (D) Tungabhadra — (Distractor): While Tungabhadra is also a shield tributary of Krishna, Krishna is the primary master river of the peninsular drainage designated in standard syllabus keys.

Q37: Global Marine Tectonics & Oceanic Ridge/Trench Geography

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: C.M.R. Fowler (The Solid Earth, 2nd Ed., Ch. 2, pp. 18-24); Kearey, Klepeis & Vine (Global Tectonics, Ch. 4)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

37.1 Global Tectonic Framework of Ocean Basins

In marine geology and global plate tectonics (C.M.R. Fowler, The Solid Earth: An Introduction to Global Geophysics, 2nd Ed., Ch. 2; Kearey, Klepeis & Vine, Global Tectonics, 3rd Ed., Ch. 4), the ocean floor is subdivided into divergent mid-ocean ridge systems, convergent subduction trenches, and transform fracture zones:

Feature Name Geotectonic Nature Actual Geographic & Ocean Basin Location Associated Tectonic Plates
Reykjanes Ridge Divergent Mid-Ocean Spreading Ridge (Segment of Mid-Atlantic Ridge) North Atlantic Ocean (southwest of Iceland, between $55^\circ\text{N}$ and $63^\circ\text{N}$). North American Plate & Eurasian Plate
Carlsberg Ridge Slow-spreading Divergent Mid-Ocean Ridge Northwestern Indian Ocean (trending SE from Gulf of Aden / Socotra towards Chagos). African Plate (Somali) & Indo-Australian Plate
Kermadec Trench Deep-sea Convergent Subduction Trench ($10,047\text{ m}$ depth) Southwestern Pacific Ocean (north of New Zealand, continuous with Tonga Trench). Pacific Plate subducting beneath Indo-Australian Plate
Phoenix Ridge (Antarctic-Phoenix) Extinct Spreading Ridge Segment Southern Pacific / Antarctic Ocean (Drake Passage / Antarctic Peninsula, NOT the Arctic Ocean!). Former Phoenix Plate & Antarctic Plate
Gakkel Ridge Ultra-slow Divergent Mid-Ocean Ridge True Arctic Ocean Spreading Ridge (between Greenland and Siberia). North American Plate & Eurasian Plate

37.2 The Arctic Ocean Spreading Center: Gakkel Ridge

The sole active spreading mid-ocean ridge in the Arctic Ocean is the Gakkel Ridge (formerly Nansen Cordillera), the slowest spreading center on Earth ($< 10\text{ mm/yr}$). The Phoenix Ridge is located at the antipodal southern extremity of the globe near the South Shetland Trench in Antarctica.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q37. Find the incorrect pair :
(A) Kermadec Trench — Pacific Ocean
(B) Reykjanes Ridge — Atlantic Ocean
(C) Phoenix Ridge — Arctic Ocean
(D) Carlsberg Ridge — Indian Ocean
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (C)

Correct Answer: (C) Phoenix Ridge — Arctic Ocean — This pair is incorrect. The Phoenix Ridge is located in the Antarctic / Southern Pacific Ocean near the Antarctic Peninsula, whereas the mid-ocean ridge of the Arctic Ocean is the Gakkel Ridge.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Kermadec Trench — Pacific Ocean — CORRECT PAIR: The Kermadec Trench is one of the deepest subduction zones on Earth, located in the South Pacific Ocean.
  • (B) Reykjanes Ridge — Atlantic Ocean — CORRECT PAIR: The Reykjanes Ridge is the prominent northern arm of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge extending directly to Iceland.
  • (C) Phoenix Ridge — Arctic Ocean — INCORRECT PAIR (The Required Answer): The Phoenix Ridge is an extinct spreading center in the Pacific-Antarctic/Drake Passage region of Antarctica, not the Arctic Ocean.
  • (D) Carlsberg Ridge — Indian Ocean — CORRECT PAIR: The Carlsberg Ridge is the principal NW-SE spreading ridge bisecting the northern Indian Ocean.

Q38: Seismology: Hypocenter (Focus), Epicenter & Isoseismal Attenuation

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Peter M. Shearer (Introduction to Seismology, Ch. 1, pp. 1-8); K.M. Bangar (Ch. 10, pp. 142-148)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

38.1 Geometric & Physical Definitions of Earthquake Origins

In observational seismology and geophysics (Peter M. Shearer, Introduction to Seismology, 2nd Ed., Ch. 1; Lowrie, Fundamentals of Geophysics, Ch. 3; Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 10), an earthquake involves the rapid release of accumulated elastic strain energy along a fault rupture surface:

Seismological Term Spatial & Geometric Definition Physical Role in Wave Dynamics Damage & Intensity Relationship
Focus (Hypocenter) The exact point inside the Earth's interior where the fault rupture nucleates and initial slip begins. Origin point of radiating spherical $P$ and $S$ body wavefronts. Subsurface point; depth ($h$) ranges from shallow ($0-70\text{ km}$) to deep ($> 300\text{ km}$).
Epicenter The point on the Earth's surface directly vertically above the focus (hypocenter). Point of initial arrival of seismic waves at the surface. Location of maximum seismic ground shaking intensity ($I_{\text{max}}$) and catastrophic structural damage for shallow crustal earthquakes.
Focal Depth ($h$) The vertical distance between the epicenter on the surface and the subsurface focus. Directly governs geometrical attenuation: $I \propto 1/\sqrt{\Delta^2 + h^2}$. Shallower focal depth = greater concentration of energy at epicenter.
Isoseismal Lines Closed contour curves connecting points on the Earth's surface experiencing equal earthquake intensity. Reflects directional radiation pattern and local geology. Form concentric rings centered around the epicenter.

38.2 Why the Epicenter Suffers Maximum Damage

Seismic energy density ($E_d$) attenuates with hypocentral distance ($R = \sqrt{\Delta^2 + h^2}$) due to geometrical spreading ($1/R^2$) and anelastic intrinsic attenuation ($e^{-\alpha R}$):

$$E_d(\Delta) \propto \frac{E_0}{\Delta^2 + h^2} \exp\left(-\frac{\omega R}{Q v}\right)$$

Where $\Delta$ is the epicentral distance. At the epicenter, epicentral distance is zero ($\Delta = 0$), so $R = h$ is at its absolute minimum possible value. Consequently, energy density, peak ground acceleration (PGA), and destructive surface wave amplitude are concentrated at the epicenter.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q38. What will be the location where an earthquake does the maximum damage ?
(A) Epicentre
(B) Focus
(C) 100 km from the epicenter
(D) Isocentre
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (A)

Correct Answer: (A) Epicentre — The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus is the Epicenter, which experiences the earliest wave arrival, highest peak ground acceleration, and maximum structural damage.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Epicentre — CORRECT: The point on the Earth's surface vertically above the focus where seismic intensity (Modified Mercalli / MSK scale) reaches its maximum ($I_{\text{max}}$).
  • (B) Focus — INCORRECT: The focus (hypocenter) is located deep underground inside the Earth's crust or mantle; damage to human civil infrastructure occurs at the Earth's surface.
  • (C) 100 km from the epicenter — INCORRECT: Seismic intensity attenuates rapidly with distance; shaking at $100\text{ km}$ is orders of magnitude weaker than at the epicenter.
  • (D) Isocentre — INCORRECT: In photogrammetry, an isocenter is the point on an aerial photograph where the bisector of the tilt angle meets the image; it is completely meaningless in seismology.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

Seismological Intensity Attenuation Problem

Practice Problem 38: Hypocentral Distance & Geometric Spreading

A shallow crustal earthquake has a focal depth of $h = 10\text{ km}$. Compare the geometrical wave amplitude at the epicenter ($\Delta_1 = 0\text{ km}$) with that at a seismic station located at an epicentral distance of $\Delta_2 = 30\text{ km}$, assuming simple spherical body wave geometrical spreading ($A \propto 1/R$).

Solution:

1. Hypocentral distance to epicenter ($R_1$):

$$R_1 = \sqrt{\Delta_1^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{0^2 + 10^2} = 10\text{ km}$$

2. Hypocentral distance to distant station ($R_2$):

$$R_2 = \sqrt{\Delta_2^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{30^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{900 + 100} = \sqrt{1000} \approx 31.62\text{ km}$$

3. Ratio of seismic wave amplitudes ($A_1 / A_2$):

$$\frac{A_{\text{epicenter}}}{A_{\text{station}}} = \frac{R_2}{R_1} = \frac{31.62}{10.0} \approx 3.16$$

The ground shaking amplitude at the epicenter is more than 3 times greater than at $30\text{ km}$ away (and energy density is $\sim 10$ times higher), explaining why maximum devastation is localized at the epicenter.

Q39: Seismic Wave Propagation (Body Waves vs. Surface Waves)

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Peter M. Shearer (Introduction to Seismology, Ch. 3, pp. 45-52); William Lowrie (Fundamentals of Geophysics, Ch. 3)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

39.1 Comprehensive Taxonomy of Elastic Seismic Waves

In global geophysics and seismology (Shearer, Introduction to Seismology, Ch. 3; Lowrie, Ch. 3; Fowler, Ch. 4), seismic disturbances generated by sudden fault slip propagate through and around the Earth as elastic waves. They are fundamentally split into two overarching categories:

Wave Classification Wave Types Included Propagation Domain Particle Motion Mechanics & Velocity
BODY WAVES Primary (P) Waves
Secondary (S) Waves		 Propagate through the 3D volume (interior body) of the Earth. P-wave: Compressional / longitudinal (particle motion parallel to propagation, passes through solids, liquids, gases; $v_p = \sqrt{\frac{K + 4/3\mu}{\rho}}$).
S-wave: Shear / transverse (particle motion perpendicular to propagation, cannot travel through liquids; $v_s = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\rho}}$).
SURFACE WAVES Rayleigh (R) Waves
Love (L) Waves		 Propagate strictly along the 2D surface boundary of the Earth; amplitude decays exponentially with depth ($e^{-kz}$). Rayleigh: Retrograde elliptical motion in vertical plane.
Love: Transverse horizontal shear motion trapped in surface waveguide.
Slower than body waves ($v_R \approx 0.92 v_s$), but produce the largest destructive amplitudes in earthquakes.

39.2 Elastic Wave Equation & Helmholtz Decomposition

By the Helmholtz decomposition theorem, any displacement vector field $\mathbf{u}$ in an isotropic elastic medium can be resolved into a dilatational scalar potential $\phi$ and a rotational vector potential $\mathbf{\psi}$:

$$\mathbf{u} = \nabla \phi + \nabla \times \mathbf{\psi}$$

Where $\nabla \phi$ yields the P-wave (curl-free dilatational body wave), and $\nabla \times \mathbf{\psi}$ yields the S-wave (divergence-free shear body wave). Because both travel through the interior volume (body) of the planet, they are collectively termed Body Waves.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q39. P and S waves are collectively called :
(A) Love waves
(B) Surface waves
(C) Body waves
(D) Rayleigh waves
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (C)

Correct Answer: (C) Body waves — $P$ (primary compressional) waves and $S$ (secondary shear) waves propagate through the interior volume of the Earth and are collectively termed Body waves.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Love waves — INCORRECT: Love waves are a specific type of horizontal shear surface wave, not a collective term for P and S waves.
  • (B) Surface waves — INCORRECT: Surface waves (Rayleigh and Love waves) are guided along the Earth's exterior surface; P and S waves travel through the interior body.
  • (C) Body waves — CORRECT: The standard, universally established geophysical term for seismic waves that penetrate the interior volume (body) of the Earth.
  • (D) Rayleigh waves — INCORRECT: Rayleigh waves are elliptical retrograde surface waves.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

High-Yield Travel-Time Problem

Practice Problem 39: Determining Epicentral Distance via P-S Wave Interval

A regional seismograph station records the first arrival of a P-wave at $10:14:20\text{ UTC}$ and the first arrival of an S-wave at $10:14:48\text{ UTC}$. If the average crustal P-wave velocity is $v_p = 6.0\text{ km/s}$ and S-wave velocity is $v_s = 3.5\text{ km/s}$, calculate the epicentral distance ($D$) to the earthquake.

Solution:

1. The time difference between the arrivals is:

$$\Delta t = t_s - t_p = 48\text{ s} - 20\text{ s} = 28\text{ seconds}$$

2. The travel time formula for body waves is:

$$\Delta t = D \left(\frac{1}{v_s} - \frac{1}{v_p}\right) = D \left(\frac{v_p - v_s}{v_p v_s}\right)$$ $$D = \Delta t \times \frac{v_p v_s}{v_p - v_s}$$

3. Substitute the values:

$$D = 28 \times \frac{6.0 \times 3.5}{6.0 - 3.5} = 28 \times \frac{21.0}{2.5} = 28 \times 8.4 = \mathbf{235.2\text{ km}}$$

The earthquake epicenter is located $235.2\text{ km}$ from the seismograph station.

Q40: Landslide Morphology: Kinematics of Displaced Mass vs. Subjacent Bedrock

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: D.J. Varnes (1978, Landslides: Analysis and Control); Cruden & Varnes (1996); K.M. Bangar (Ch. 12)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

40.1 Varnes (1978) Morphological Anatomy of a Landslide

In geotechnical engineering and engineering geology (Cruden & Varnes, 1996; Varnes, 1978; Bangar, Principles of Engineering Geology, Ch. 12), a landslide is defined as the downslope movement of a mass of rock, debris, or earth under the direct influence of gravity. The slope is partitioned by a distinct surface of rupture (shear plane) into two mechanically distinct masses:

Zonal Component Physical Description & Terminology Mechanical State & Factor of Safety ($FS$) Geotechnical Stability
Displaced Mass (Mass Above Slip Surface) The volume of rock or soil that has broken away from the parent slope and moved downslope along or beyond the surface of rupture. Shear stress exceeded shear strength ($\tau > \tau_f$); $FS < 1.0$. Highly fractured, remolded, dilation occurred; lost cohesive bond. UNSTABLE / ACTIVELY DEFORMING
Subjacent Mass (Mass Below Slip Surface) The intact, undisturbed rock or soil mass situated beneath the surface of rupture and forming the stable foundation/bedrock. Resisting shear strength intact; $\tau < \tau_f$; $FS > 1.0$. Preserves native confinement and structural integrity. STABLE / INTACT

40.2 Mohr-Coulomb Rupture Localization

The failure occurs along the surface of rupture when driving stresses overcome shear resistance:

$$\tau_f = c' + (\sigma_n - u) \tan \phi'$$

The mass above the rupture surface experiences loss of shear strength, catastrophic displacement, and extensive disaggregation, rendering it unstable. The mass below the surface of rupture remains fully anchored to the autochthonous geological formation, remaining completely stable.

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q40. What is the distinguishing feature of the mass above and below a landslide ?
(A) Both masses are stable
(B) Mass above is stable, whereas mass below is unstable
(C) Mass above is unstable, whereas mass below is stable
(D) Both masses are unstable
VERIFIED ANSWER: OPTION (C)

Correct Answer: (C) Mass above is unstable, whereas mass below is stable — In landslide kinematics, the displaced mass situated above the shear failure plane is mechanically unstable, while the underlying intact bedrock mass situated below the slip plane is stable.

Option-by-Option Critical Dissection

  • (A) Both masses are stable — INCORRECT: If both were stable, no landslide failure or downslope movement could ever take place.
  • (B) Mass above is stable, whereas mass below is unstable — INCORRECT: Complete inversion of physical reality; the displaced material that slides downslope is above the slip surface, not below it.
  • (C) Mass above is unstable, whereas mass below is stable — CORRECT: Precisely captures the mechanical demarcation defined by the basal shear rupture surface (Varnes 1978).
  • (D) Both masses are unstable — INCORRECT: The underlying deep bedrock below the shear plane is not in a state of sliding failure; it forms the stable substrate across which the slide moves.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

High-Yield Slope Remediation Table

Engineering Remediation Method Target Landslide Zone Mechanical Principle
Rock Anchors & Fully Grouted Dowels Drilled through unstable upper mass into stable lower mass Pins the unstable slide mass securely to the stable bedrock, increasing normal stress and shear resistance.
Horizontal Drainage Bores Punctures the slip surface into the upper mass Dissipates pore water pressure ($u$), increasing effective stress $\sigma_n' = (\sigma_n - u)$.
Toe Bench / Retaining Gabion Wall Base of unstable displaced mass Provides passive resisting force ($P_p$) against driving gravitational moment.
