Q145: Coastal Hydrogeology - Geometry of the Fresh-Saline Water Interface

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: R.E. Glover (1959, The Pattern of Fresh-Water Flow in a Coastal Aquifer); Todd & Mays (Ch. 14)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Interface Geometry

Question 145: Choose the correct answer regarding the shape and the nature of the fresh water-saline water interface near to a coastal area from the options given below :

  • (A) Linear and horizontal
  • (B) Concave upward
  • (C) Linear and inclined
  • (D) Convex downward

Correct Answer: (B) Concave upward

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q145. Choose the correct answer regarding the shape and the nature of the fresh water-saline water interface near to a coastal area from the options given below :
(A) Linear and horizontal
(B) Concave upward
(C) Linear and inclined
(D) Convex downward

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: The Ghyben-Herzberg & Glover Coastal Interface

In coastal aquifers, freshwater originating from inland recharge flows toward the sea, floating above denser seawater (freshwater density $\rho_f = 1.000\text{ g/cm}^3$; seawater density $\rho_s = 1.025\text{ g/cm}^3$):

  • The Classical Ghyben-Herzberg Relation: Under hydrostatic equilibrium: $$z = \frac{\rho_f}{\rho_s - \rho_f} h_f \approx 40 h_f$$ where $h_f$ is the freshwater water table height above sea level, and $z$ is the depth of the interface below sea level. Every 1 meter of freshwater head above sea level supports 40 meters of freshwater column below sea level.
  • Dynamic Glover (1959) Parabolic Interface:
    • In real aquifers, freshwater is discharging dynamically into the sea at an exit face on the seafloor.
    • Because freshwater flowlines converge toward the coastal discharge zone, vertical hydraulic gradients develop near the shore.
    • Mathematical solution of the flow net (Glover's equation) demonstrates that the dynamic interface profile is a parabola described by: $$z^2 = \frac{2 Q x}{K \Delta \rho / \rho_f} + \left(\frac{Q}{K \Delta \rho / \rho_f}\right)^2$$
    • This parabolic curve has a concave upward curvature (curving gently downward inland and steepening upward as it approaches the shoreline/seafloor).

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (Concave upward) is correct: The rigorous dynamic Glover-Hubbert parabolic profile of the fresh-saline interface.
  • Option A (Linear and horizontal): Static planar layer, impossible in dynamic discharging coastal aquifers.
  • Option C (Linear and inclined): Oversimplified hydrostatic approximation that ignores shoreline flow convergence.
  • Option D (Convex downward): Inverted curvature, physically incorrect for a lighter fluid discharging over a denser fluid wedge.

Q146: Well Hydraulics - Pumping Period vs Recovery Period Terminology

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: C.V. Theis (1935, Recovery of Drawdown in Pumping Tests); Todd & Mays (Ch. 4)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Aquifer Test Phases

Question 146: Find out the term which is not related to the pumping period of a well :

  • (A) Drawdown
  • (B) Time-drawdown data
  • (C) Residual drawdown
  • (D) Distance-drawdown data

Correct Answer: (C) Residual drawdown

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q146. Find out the term which is not related to the pumping period of a well :
(A) Drawdown
(B) Time-drawdown data
(C) Residual drawdown
(D) Distance-drawdown data

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Pumping Tests vs Recovery Tests

An aquifer test is divided into two distinct, sequential operational phases:

Operational Phase Well Activity State Key Measurements & Hydraulic Curves
1. Pumping Period ($0 \le t \le t_p$) The pump runs continuously at a constant discharge rate $Q$. • Drawdown ($s$): The decline in piezometric head below initial static water level ($s = h_0 - h$).
• Time-drawdown data: Measurements of increasing drawdown versus elapsed pumping time ($s$ vs $t$).
• Distance-drawdown data: Measurements of drawdown recorded simultaneously across multiple observation wells at various radial distances ($s$ vs $r$).
2. Recovery Period ($t' > 0$, after $t_p$) The pump is shut off ($Q = 0$); water levels rebound toward original static levels. • Residual Drawdown ($s'$): The difference between the original pre-pumping static water level and the recovering water level at time $t'$ after pumping stopped.
Analyzed using Theis's Recovery Method: $$s' = \frac{2.3 Q}{4\pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{t}{t'}\right)$$

Because residual drawdown is measured strictly and exclusively during the recovery period after the pump has been switched off, it is NOT related to the pumping period of a well.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option C (Residual drawdown) is correct: Exclusively defines the post-pumping recovery phase.
  • Options A, B, and D: Core parameters gathered and plotted during active pumping.

Q147: The Cooper-Jacob Method - Boundary Conditions & Validity Limits

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: H.H. Cooper & C.E. Jacob (1946, Generalized Graphical Method for Evaluating Formation Constants)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Analytical Validity

Question 147: Conditions under which Jacob-Cooper method cannot be used for analysis of pump test data :
(i) When the pump test is of short duration
(ii) When the pump test is of long duration
(iii) When the observation well is situated far away from the main well
(iv) When the observation well is situated nearer to the main well
Choose the correct set of answer from the following :

  • (A) (i) and (iii)
  • (B) (ii) and (iii)
  • (C) (ii) and (iv)
  • (D) (i) and (iv)

Correct Answer: (A) (i) and (iii)

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q147. Conditions under which Jacob-Cooper method cannot be used for analysis of pump test data : (i) When the pump test is of short duration, (ii) When the pump test is of long duration, (iii) When the observation well is situated far away from the main well, (iv) When the observation well is situated nearer to the main well. Choose the correct set of answer from the following :
(A) (i) and (iii)
(B) (ii) and (iii)
(C) (ii) and (iv)
(D) (i) and (iv)

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: The Cooper-Jacob Straight-Line Approximation

The Theis (1935) non-equilibrium equation models transient radial drawdown in a confined aquifer:

$$s = \frac{Q}{4\pi T} W(u) = \frac{Q}{4\pi T} \left( -0.5772 - \ln u + u - \frac{u^2}{2 \cdot 2!} + \cdots \right)$$ where the Boltzmann variable $u$ is defined as: $$u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t}$$
  • The Cooper-Jacob (1946) Simplification:
    • Cooper and Jacob recognized that when $u$ is sufficiently small ($u \le 0.01$ to $0.05$), the higher-order terms in the infinite series become negligible.
    • Under this condition, the exponential integral simplifies to a straight line on semi-logarithmic paper: $$s \approx \frac{2.3 Q}{4\pi T} \log_{10}\left(\frac{2.25 T t}{r^2 S}\right)$$
  • When Cooper-Jacob CANNOT Be Used ($u > 0.05$): The method fails and yields gross errors whenever $u$ is large: $$u = \frac{r^2 S}{4 T t} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad u \text{ is large when } \begin{cases} t \text{ is small (short duration of pumping, Condition i)} \\ r \text{ is large (observation well far away, Condition iii)} \end{cases}$$
  • Therefore, the Cooper-Jacob straight-line approximation cannot be used when the test is of short duration (i) or when the observation well is located far from the pumped well (iii).

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option A ((i) and (iii)) is correct: Small $t$ and large $r$ make $u > 0.05$, violating the mathematical truncation assumption.
  • Condition (ii) & (iv): Long duration ($t$ large) and close observation well ($r$ small) produce small $u$, which is the ideal condition where Cooper-Jacob works perfectly.

Q148: Water Well Drilling - Cable Tool Percussion in the Bhabar Piedmont

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Hydrogeological Drilling Technique

Question 148: The suitable method of drilling in the Piedmont zone (Bhabar) occurring adjacent to the Himalayan foothills is :

  • (A) Rotary method
  • (B) Cable tool method
  • (C) Reverse rotary method
  • (D) Air rotary method

Correct Answer: (B) Cable tool method

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q148. The suitable method of drilling in the Piedmont zone (Bhabar) occurring adjacent to the Himalayan foothills is :
(A) Rotary method
(B) Cable tool method
(C) Reverse rotary method
(D) Air rotary method

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Drilling Challenges in the Himalayan Bhabar Piedmont

The Bhabar zone is a high-energy piedmont alluvial fan belt skirting the southern foot of the Siwalik hills across the Indo-Gangetic margin:

  • Formidable Lithological Formation: Composed of unstratified, highly porous, permeable deposits of loose boulders, quartzitic cobbles, gravels, and coarse sand with very deep water tables ($>30 - 60\text{ m}$).
  • Why Rotary Drilling Fails Catastrophically in Bhabar:
    • Direct and Reverse Rotary: Drilling fluid (bentonite mud or water) immediately drains away into the cavernous inter-boulder voids, causing total lost circulation. Unconsolidated boulders roll against the rotating bit, jamming drill strings and collapsing hole walls.
  • Superiority of Cable Tool (Percussion) Drilling:
    • Operates by repeatedly lifting and dropping a heavy chisel-shaped percussion bit attached to a wire cable ($30 - 60\text{ strokes/min}$).
    • The crushing blows shatter quartzite boulders in-situ, while a heavy steel drive casing is driven downward simultaneously just behind the bit.
    • The casing prevents hole caving and eliminates the need for circulating drilling mud. Pulverized slurry is bailed out cleanly with a dart-valve bailer.
  • The Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) and hydrogeological drilling standards officially prescribe Cable Tool percussion drilling as the time-tested, most reliable drilling technique in the rugged Bhabar boulder formation.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (Cable tool method) is correct: The proven percussion method with concurrent casing drive for boulder-cobble gravel piedmonts.
  • Option A (Rotary method): Suffers total fluid circulation loss and severe bit jamming in loose gravel/boulder formations.
  • Option C (Reverse rotary): Requires huge volumes of standing water and stable clay cake, impossible in porous Bhabar gravels.
  • Option D (Air rotary): Uncased air rotary causes massive wall collapse in unconsolidated boulders.

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: Sam Boggs Jr. (Principles of Sedimentology and Stratigraphy, Ch. 3, p. 60); Todd & Mays

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Granulometric Aquifer Selection

Question 149: After completion of drilling of a water well, four different aquifer zones with the following textural characteristics have been demarcated. Select the most promise zone for withdrawl of groundwater :
(A) Zone I : Effective size value 0.55 mm and uniformity coefficient 3.60
(B) Zone II : Effective size value 0.75 mm and uniformity coefficient 2.10
(C) Zone III : Effective size value 0.65 mm and uniformity coefficient 2.60
(D) Zone IV : Effective size value 0.75 mm and uniformity coefficient 3.70

  • (A) Zone I
  • (B) Zone II
  • (C) Zone III
  • (D) Zone IV

Correct Answer: (B) Zone II : Effective size value 0.75 mm and uniformity coefficient 2.10

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q149. After completion of drilling of a water well, four different aquifer zones with the following textural characteristics have been demarcated. Select the most promise zone for withdrawl of groundwater : (A) Zone I : Effective size value 0.55 mm and uniformity coefficient 3.60, (B) Zone II : Effective size value 0.75 mm and uniformity coefficient 2.10, (C) Zone III : Effective size value 0.65 mm and uniformity coefficient 2.60, (D) Zone IV : Effective size value 0.75 mm and uniformity coefficient 3.70
(A) Zone I
(B) Zone II
(C) Zone III
(D) Zone IV

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Aquifer Textural Parameters and Well Yield

The hydraulic conductivity ($K$), specific yield, and well screen design of an unconsolidated sand aquifer are strictly dictated by two granulometric parameters derived from sieve analysis:

  1. Effective Grain Size ($D_{10}$):
    • The sieve diameter through which $10\%$ of the sediment mass passes.
    • According to Hazen's formula ($K = C \cdot D_{10}^2$), hydraulic conductivity is directly proportional to the square of effective size. A larger $D_{10}$ signifies substantially larger pore throat diameters, drastically reducing frictional resistance to fluid flow.
    • Comparing the candidate zones, $D_{10} = 0.75\text{ mm}$ (Zones II and IV) is far superior to $0.55\text{ mm}$ and $0.65\text{ mm}$.
  2. Uniformity Coefficient ($C_u$):
    • Defined as $C_u = \frac{D_{60}}{D_{10}}$.
    • $C_u$ measures the sorting and gradation of the sand. A lower $C_u$ ($< 2.5$) indicates a highly uniform, well-sorted sand where grain sizes are nearly identical.
    • A higher $C_u$ ($> 3.5$) indicates poorly sorted, well-graded sand where smaller particles fill the voids between larger grains, dramatically choking porosity and choking hydraulic permeability!

Synthesis for Zone Selection:
Both Zone II and Zone IV have the highest effective size ($D_{10} = 0.75\text{ mm}$). However, Zone II has $C_u = 2.10$ (well-sorted, open packing, high permeability), whereas Zone IV has $C_u = 3.70$ (poorly sorted, interstitial clogging by finer grains). Therefore, Zone II is unequivocally the most promising aquifer zone for groundwater withdrawal.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option B (Zone II) is correct: Combines maximum coarse effective size ($D_{10} = 0.75\text{ mm}$) with superior sorting ($C_u = 2.10$).
  • Option D (Zone IV): While $D_{10}$ is $0.75\text{ mm}$, high $C_u = 3.70$ indicates poorly sorted grains with fine matrix clogging pore channels.
  • Option A & C: Substantially smaller effective grain sizes ($0.55\text{ mm}$ and $0.65\text{ mm}$).

Q150: Hydrochemistry - Electrical Conductivity (EC) to TDS Conversion

Exam: Geology Paper-II (2021)  |  Authoritative Reference: J.D. Hem (Study and Interpretation of the Chemical Characteristics of Natural Water, USGS WSP 2254)

Part I: Theoretical Foundation & Concept Masterclass

1. Question & Standard Hydrochemical Conversion

Question 150: Water with electrical conductivity value of 2500 micro siemens/cm (at 25°C) is considered suitable for drinking purpose. When expressed this drinking water standard in terms of TDS, the corresponding TDS value (in mg/l) would become :

  • (A) 1500 mg/l
  • (B) 1550 mg/l
  • (C) 1600 mg/l
  • (D) 1650 mg/l

Correct Answer: (C) 1600 mg/l

Part II: Official Question & Critical Option Dissection

Q150. Water with electrical conductivity value of 2500 micro siemens/cm (at 25°C) is considered suitable for drinking purpose. When expressed this drinking water standard in terms of TDS, the corresponding TDS value (in mg/l) would become :
(A) 1500 mg/l
(B) 1550 mg/l
(C) 1600 mg/l
(D) 1650 mg/l

2. Detailed Geological Masterclass: Hydrochemical Correlation between EC and TDS

Electrical Conductivity (EC) measures the ability of water to conduct an electric current, directly proportional to the concentration of dissolved ionized mineral salts. Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) represents the total mass of dissolved inorganic minerals expressed in milligrams per liter ($ ext{mg/l}$):

  • The Empirical Conversion Equation: $$\text{TDS (mg/l)} = A \times \text{EC (}\mu\text{S/cm at } 25^\circ\text{C)}$$ where $A$ is an empirical conversion factor determined by the dominant dissolved ionic species.
  • Standard Hydrochemical Values of Factor $A$:
    • For fresh waters dominated by bicarbonate, $A \approx 0.55 - 0.60$.
    • For mixed and moderately mineralized waters, $A \approx 0.64 - 0.65$ (the USGS standard factor established by Hem, 1985; Water-Supply Paper 2254).
    • For saline waters rich in sulfate and chloride, $A \approx 0.70 - 0.80$.
  • Calculation for the Exam Parameter: $$\text{Given: } \text{EC} = 2500\,\mu\text{S/cm}$$ Using the standard empirical multiplier $A = 0.64$: $$\text{TDS} = 2500 \times 0.64 = \mathbf{1600\text{ mg/l}}$$ This matches Option (C) exactly.

Part III: Synthesis Reference Tables & High-Yield Practice

3. Critical Option Elimination & Exam Traps

  • Option C (1600 mg/l) is correct: $2500\,\mu\text{S/cm} \times 0.64 = 1600\text{ mg/l}$, matching the standard hydrochemical conversion coefficient.
  • Option A (1500 mg/l): Corresponds to $A = 0.60$, which understates mineralization for a high $2500\,\mu\text{S/cm}$ water.
  • Option B & D: Off-target multipliers ($0.62$ and $0.66$).
